summary: Sets out terminology, an abstract framework and goals for content negotiation that does not depend on any one protocol. It also identifies technical issues needing more work. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Content negotiation is how a sender and a receiver agree on which version of a file to send, when several versions exist. RFC 2703 sets out the words for that conversation and a framework for it that does not depend on any one protocol, so e-mail, the web and directory lookups could all use the same ideas.

questions: what is a feature set in content negotiation
what is protocol independent content negotiation
subtitle: A shared vocabulary and framework for agreeing on which version of a resource to send

tldr.problem: Many application protocols need to agree on which version of a resource to transfer. MIME media types handle one axis of variation, but resources also vary in ways that current MIME headers cannot express.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the vocabulary of negotiation, then separates an abstract negotiation process and an abstract metadata model from the concrete representations and protocol bindings, so any application protocol can plug in underneath.
tldr.outcome: The result is a framework and a list of goals rather than a protocol. The memo leaves open the harder questions of streamed data, hop-by-hop negotiation, third parties such as directories, billing and performance, and catalogues the security risks.

today: RFC 2703 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a framework document, not a protocol: it fixes the vocabulary and the goals and lists the questions that a protocol-specific binding would still have to answer.

sections.title: Why Protocol-Independent Content Negotiation
sections.content:
Many Internet application protocols need to negotiate content for the resources they work with. MIME media types give a standard way to handle one major axis of variation, but resources also vary in ways that current MIME headers cannot express.

The memo therefore sets out terminology, an abstract framework and goals for protocol-independent content negotiation, and points out technical issues that may need attention. It does not try to specify the negotiation process itself; it indicates the scope and form that such a specification might take. The goals are the desired properties of a negotiation mechanism, written so that no particular shape of framework is assumed.

Discussion of the memo was to take place on the content negotiation and media feature registration mailing list hosted by the Internet Mail Consortium, and the memo says it was informed by the debates of the IETF conneg working group.
sections.plainLanguage: When one computer can send a file in several forms, sender and receiver have to agree on which form to use. RFC 2703 gives the vocabulary for that agreement and a general shape for it, so that the idea can work the same way in e-mail, in the web and in directory lookups.

sections.title: The Vocabulary
sections.content:
The memo's second section defines the terms used with a special meaning, many of them copied and adapted from the Transparent Content Negotiation work, and lists them alphabetically.

The core of the vocabulary is the variant: one of several possible representations of a data resource. A data resource may be available in several representations, for example multiple languages, data formats, sizes or resolutions. A variant resource is a data resource for which several representations are available, and a negotiable resource is one where the variant to transmit is selected by negotiating between sender and recipient. The variant list holds descriptions of the variants, and a variant description contains a variant resource identifier plus attributes describing the properties of that variant.

On the capabilities side, a feature is a piece of information about the media handling properties of a component or a resource, and a feature tag is the name that identifies it. A feature set is the full set of features that a sender, a recipient or a data file can handle. A capability is an attribute indicating an ability to generate or process a particular type of content, a characteristic indicates a possible capability or preference, and a preference says which of two possible contents is wanted. Negotiation metadata is the information that sender and receiver exchange in order to work out which variant should be transferred.

Two kinds of message are named. A list message sends the variant list but no variant data, and can be generated when the sender does not want to, or is not allowed to, send a particular variant. A choice message returns a representation of the selected variant, or variants, together with the variant list, and needs the receiver to be told what else was on offer. The memo also distinguishes sender-initiated transmission, which is push, from receiver-initiated transmission, which is pull, giving an HTTP GET operation as an example of the latter.
sections.plainLanguage: The words matter here. A variant is one version of a resource, such as the same report in two languages. A feature set is the list of things a computer can handle, and negotiation metadata is the information both sides swap to agree on a version. The memo also names the two obvious moves: a list message that offers the versions without sending one, and a choice message that sends a version and still says what else there was.

sections.title: The Abstract Framework
sections.content:
The framework covers three things: expressing the capabilities of the sender and of the data resource to be transmitted, expressing the capabilities of a receiver before the transmission, and a protocol by which capabilities are exchanged.

The memo draws the design elements and their dependencies. An abstract negotiation process and an abstract negotiation metadata model sit above a negotiation protocol binding and a negotiation metadata representation, and all of it is used by an application protocol that incorporates content negotiation. Protocol independence comes from keeping the abstract process and the metadata apart from concrete representations and protocol bindings. The capabilities of the transmission protocol itself are deliberately disregarded, on the assumption that they are handled separately by some orthogonal mechanism.

To show where the negotiation sits, the memo gives the life of a data resource: an author produces original document content, a sending system transmits a data file that is a representation of that content, a receiving system renders it into formatted document data, and a user consumes the result. It is the sending system and the receiving system that exchange negotiation metadata to decide the form of the data file. The sender's metadata reflects which variants of the content exist and what formats it can offer them in; the receiver's metadata reflects the needs and preferences of its user and what it is able to process.

The negotiation itself is a series of metadata exchanges that continues until either side settles on a specific data file. If the sender makes the final choice it can send the file directly; otherwise the receiver must communicate its selection and the sender sends what was chosen. Every concrete negotiation is expected to be a subset of that general process: Transparent Content Negotiation, for example, covers a request with no variants, a request that gets a list of variants back so the client can choose, and a request that carries the client's own metadata so the server can choose on its behalf. Fax negotiation is a simpler case where the recipient declares its capabilities and the sender picks a variant to match.

The metadata model then has to cover six things: a way to describe attributes of a data resource, called a media feature; a description of a range of possible media feature combinations, called a feature set; one or more naming schemes for labelling media features and feature sets, backed by a registration process that keeps names unique and encourages a shared vocabulary; a framework of data types giving the range and properties of the values that can be represented; a way to combine media features into feature sets that can express dependencies inside a set, such as 640x480 pixels with 256 colours or 800x600 pixels with 16 colours; and some way of ranking feature sets by the preferences of sender and receiver. A textual representation would give text-based protocols such as HTTP and SMTP a shared vocabulary, and an ASN.1 description would help protocols built on ASN.1, such as X.400, X.500, LDAP and SNMP; separate media feature naming based on ISO object identifiers would be valuable for that. Concrete protocol bindings will be needed, though their details are out of scope, and the memo notes that SASL might provide a useful model.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework has three moving parts: what the sender can offer, what the receiver can accept, and the protocol used to swap that information. Above them sits the idea of an abstract negotiation process, which can be bound to any application protocol. The memo shows where the talking happens by drawing the life of a document: an author writes it, a sending system picks a form, a receiving system renders it, and a user reads it. The two systems in the middle are the ones that negotiate.

sections.title: Goals for a Negotiation Framework
sections.content:
The goals fall into two groups. The generic goals address negotiation in a protocol-independent way: a common vocabulary for designating features and feature sets; a stable reference for commonly used features; an extensible framework so new features can be adopted quickly; a way to indicate quality or preference; a way to capture dependencies between feature values; a uniform mechanism for exchanging metadata that covers existing features and can grow to meet unanticipated ones; efficient negotiation in both pull and push transfers; a structure that stands independently of any particular message transfer protocol; and the ability to serve the communication needs of less able computer users.

The protocol-specific goals are for whoever writes the binding for a particular protocol. A negotiation should generally end with a form of data that both sides accept. Capabilities sent outside a transfer should carry enough information to be verified and authenticated, and a capability assertion should name the party the capabilities apply to, the party they are sent to, and their date or range of validity, protected against interception and substitution. A request for capabilities should name the requester, the party whose capabilities are asked for and the time of the request. There should be a standardised way to associate features with resource variants, and a way to show provider and recipient preferences. Negotiation should have as little effect as possible on network resources, especially bandwidth and round-trips. Systems should protect the privacy of user profiles and provider inventories, and protocols should allow the accuracy of capability data to be checked. Negotiation must not jeopardise the operation or integrity of a system when the capability data is wrong, whether that happens by accident or attack. Gateways, proxies and caches should be allowed to take part, and the metadata should be regarded as cacheable with explicit cache control provided, so that ad-hoc cache-busting techniques do not creep in. Finally, automatic negotiation should not take away the user's ability to choose a document format from those available.
sections.plainLanguage: The goals read like a wish list. There should be one shared vocabulary for features, new features should be easy to add, and the whole thing should work the same whether the transfer is push or pull. It should cost as little bandwidth and round-trips as possible, it must not break a system when the data it is given is wrong, and it must not quietly decide the format for the user.

sections.title: Open Technical Issues
sections.content:
The memo lists questions it does not answer. The ideas for generic content negotiation were conceived in the context of message-oriented transfers, where the content is settled before transmission starts; streamed data, interactive computations and real-time data acquisition are not, and it may be that the metadata still applies but the abstract process is not enough for them.

There is also the question of end-to-end against hop-by-hop negotiation. End-to-end gives the greatest confidence in the outcome. Hop-by-hop may have advantages in a network of occasionally connected systems, but puts additional demands on the intervening message transmission agents, and a hop-by-hop response is not necessarily a definitive indication of the endpoint's capabilities, which implies a possible need for time-to-live and re-verification mechanisms to flush out stale negotiation data. Allowing a third party, such as a directory service using LDAP, to supply negotiation metadata increases the ways errors can be introduced, and steps are needed to keep it reliable; using LDAP to carry the metadata also means defining schema elements specific to content negotiation, for instance an attribute type for a media feature set.

Two further issues are raised. Negotiation may raise billing questions, because it can involve a two-way exchange of data that is not completed within a single connection, so somebody has to pay for the return messages, as in e-mail or fax. On performance, negotiation can help or hurt: the extra data costs bandwidth, and the metadata exchange adds round-trip or third-party query delays before transmission of the message itself starts, but in Internet e-mail the multipart/alternative type buys latency with bandwidth by sending several versions of a resource, while HTTP suggests a mechanism that buys bandwidth at the cost of a round-trip. And on confidence, the parties may be certain of the outcome after a direct exchange, or working from a best guess that the recipient should be able to reject. The memo points to the pattern used by Transparent Content Negotiation, where a procedure guarantees a correct outcome and an optimisation uses easily obtained but less reliable information while keeping checks that guarantee the same final result.
sections.plainLanguage: Several questions are left open. The framework was built around messages, where everything is settled before sending starts, so streamed or live data may need something more. Negotiating end to end is the most reliable, but letting each router in between help out saves work and makes the answer less definite. Using a directory service to carry the negotiation details is convenient but adds a new way for things to go wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo catalogues security issues that negotiation protocols should consider. Privacy can be harmed by the unintended disclosure of personal information, and by spoofed requests for negotiation data made only to gather information rather than as part of a real transfer. Service denial can be caused by injecting false negotiation data or by making excessive requests for it.

Content negotiation with final recipients is somewhat at odds with the normal practice of keeping the identities and addresses of mailing list subscribers confidential, so end-to-end negotiation through a mailing list is not consistent with good security practice. Protocols that use security services for message transfer should apply those services to negotiation as well: authenticated requests let a potential recipient moderate the distribution of media capability information, authentication of the metadata stops a sender being misled by data injected by another party, encryption may prevent the disclosure of sensitive capability information to snoopers, and conducting the exchange over an authenticated or encrypted protocol session or network path can give both parties mutual authentication.

Three disclosure risks are named. Capability information may let an attacker deduce which message handling agent is in use and so lead to the exploitation of known weaknesses in that agent. Knowing which applications a recipient employs, for example from the file format, may assist an attack, although macro viruses can be spread without such knowledge by sending multiple messages, each of which infects a specific application version. And because one use of content negotiation is to deliver content meeting the requirements of less able people, disclosing that information may make those people targets for attacks that play on their personal vulnerabilities. Finally, if feature negotiation is used to decide which security-related features to use, a subverted negotiation procedure could prevent effective security procedures from being selected; the memo points to the security considerations of GSS-API negotiation for the use of integrity protecting mechanisms with security negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: Negotiation can leak information about the person on the other end, so requests for it should be authenticated and the answers protected. It can also be abused: false data or too many requests can tie up a server. Telling a network what software someone runs may help an attacker, and so may revealing that someone needs an accessible format. And if negotiation is allowed to choose the security features, a manipulated negotiation could pick weak ones.
